raw_response:
I am not going to spread myself too thin. The wheat-maize land feeds the house and gives steady cash, so I will keep that as the backbone. Cotton can still bring money if the price is decent, but it takes more picking labor, so I will not put too much land there because some people in my family work outside. Mungbean does not need as much money or water, so I keep a small piece for safety. I do things mostly the way that has worked for me before. If I have cash, I would rather put a little more fertilizer on wheat and maize than be short and watch the crop turn weak. But I also cannot spend all the money at once, so on cotton and mungbean I stay tighter.

For wheat, I will keep the usual management: sow in early October, put base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress once when it starts growing strong in spring. If the winter and spring stay dry, I will use the well three times because wheat here cannot rely on the sky alone. After wheat harvest in June, I will hurry and plant summer maize right away on the same land. There is no time for fancy tillage then, just quick residue handling and planting. Cotton I will put on the better-drained piece and manage it steadily, but I will not chase very high yield because labor is short. Mungbean I treat as a low-cost crop: simple seed, not much fertilizer, and only spray if insects get bad.
